lead: This unit studies two or more random variables together: their joint law, the marginals and conditionals inside it, independence, and covariance. It then proves the two limit theorems that make statistics work — the law of large numbers and the central limit theorem — and ends with the multivariate normal.
about: The unit starts with 4.1 Joint distributions of two random variables, which builds the joint pmf, pdf and CDF of a pair (X, Y). 4.2 Marginal and conditional distributions shows how to read one variable alone, or given the other. 4.3 Independent random variables turns the joint into a product. 4.4 Covariance of two random variables measures how the pair move together and adds the correlation coefficient. The last three chapters change scale from two variables to many observations: 4.5 Law of large numbers says the sample mean settles near μ, 4.6 Central limit theorem says the error around μ is roughly normal, and 4.7 Multivariate normal distribution packages the normal idea for whole vectors. It needs Unit 2 throughout and feeds Unit 5 and Unit 6.

chapters.idea: Two random variables live together on a plane of pairs, and one function — the joint pmf, pdf or CDF — gives the probability of every region in that plane.
chapters.depth: Discrete case: joint pmf p(x,y) = P(X = x, Y = y), with p ≥ 0 and ΣΣ p = 1. Continuous case: joint pdf f(x,y), with P((X,Y) ∈ A) = ∬_A f(x,y) dx dy, f ≥ 0 and ∬ f = 1. Joint CDF F(x,y) = P(X ≤ x, Y ≤ y) and its properties: non-decreasing in each argument, right-continuous, tending to 0 at the edges and to 1 at +∞. Probability over rectangles and over curved regions such as a triangle. The support of the pair. Joint distribution of U = g(X,Y), V = h(X,Y) by the Jacobian method: f_UV(u,v) = f_XY(x,y)/|J|, where J = ∂(u,v)/∂(x,y). Some syllabi call this a two-dimensional random variable or a bivariate distribution.

figure.title: Joint pmf p(x,y) for two rolls of a die
figure.aria: A three by three table of joint probabilities for the counts of 1s and 2s in two die rolls, with the cell for one 1 and one 2 picked out.

chapters.example: A fair die is rolled twice. X = number of 1s, Y = number of 2s. The pairs with x + y ≤ 2 have p(0,0) = 16/36, p(1,0) = 8/36, p(0,1) = 8/36, p(1,1) = 2/36, p(2,0) = 1/36, p(0,2) = 1/36, and all other pairs have probability 0. Find P(X = 1, Y = 1) and P(X + Y ≥ 1). Answer: p(1,1) = 2·(1/6)(1/6) = 2/36 = 1/18 ≈ 0.056. P(X + Y ≥ 1) = 1 − p(0,0) = 1 − 16/36 = 5/9 ≈ 0.556.
chapters.trap: Treating a joint pdf value as a probability. Only a double integral over an area gives probability, and a single point has probability 0 in the continuous case. Second trap: dropping the bounds of the region while integrating, so a triangle is integrated as a rectangle.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2: random variables, pmf, pdf, CDF, expectation.
chapters.leave: Marginals and conditionals go to 4.2, independence to 4.3, covariance and correlation to 4.4, and the regression line to Unit 1.

chapters.idea: Summing or integrating the joint over one variable leaves the other alone, and dividing the joint by that marginal gives the conditional law of the other.
chapters.depth: Marginal pmf p_X(x) = Σ_y p(x,y) and marginal pdf f_X(x) = ∫ f(x,y) dy. Conditional pmf p(x|y) = p(x,y)/p_Y(y) and conditional pdf f(x|y) = f(x,y)/f_Y(y), defined only where the denominator is positive. Conditional CDF. Conditional expectation E[X|Y = y] = Σ x p(x|y) or ∫ x f(x|y) dx, conditional variance, and the total expectation rule E[X] = E[E[X|Y]]. Reading a marginal straight off the margins of a joint table.

figure.aria: Flow from the joint density to the marginal of Y by integration, then to the conditional density of X given Y by division.

chapters.example: f(x,y) = 2 for 0 < x < y < 1, and 0 elsewhere. Find both marginals, f(x|y), and E[X|Y = y]. Answer: f_Y(y) = ∫₀^y 2 dx = 2y for 0 < y < 1; f_X(x) = ∫_x^1 2 dy = 2(1 − x) for 0 < x < 1; f(x|y) = 2/(2y) = 1/y for 0 < x < y. Then E[X|Y = y] = ∫₀^y x(1/y) dx = y/2. Check with total expectation: E[X] = ∫₀^1 x·2(1 − x) dx = 1/3, and E[Y/2] = (1/2)(2/3) = 1/3.
chapters.trap: Dividing by the wrong marginal — the conditional of X given Y always divides by f_Y, never f_X. Also losing the support: 1/y is correct only for 0 < x < y, not for all x.
chapters.leave: Independence as the special case where the conditional equals the marginal is 4.3; conditional laws inside the normal model are 4.7.

chapters.idea: Two variables are independent when knowing one tells you nothing about the other, which means the joint is exactly the product of the marginals at every point.
chapters.depth: Definition: p(x,y) = p_X(x) p_Y(y) for all x, y in the discrete case, and f(x,y) = f_X(x) f_Y(y) in the continuous case. The support must be a product of intervals, a rectangle; a triangular support forces dependence. Conditional equals marginal under independence. The consequence E[g(X)h(Y)] = E[g(X)]E[h(Y)], and hence E[XY] = E[X]E[Y]. Independence of n variables, independence of families of events, and pairwise versus mutual independence. Checking independence three ways: from a table, from a formula, and from the shape of the support.

figure.aria: A decision flow: compare the joint density with the product of the two marginals; agreement on a rectangular support gives independence, otherwise dependence.

chapters.example: f(x,y) = 6e^(−2x−3y) for x > 0, y > 0. The marginals are f_X(x) = 2e^(−2x) and f_Y(y) = 3e^(−3y), and their product is 6e^(−2x−3y), so X and Y are independent. Then P(X > 1, Y > 2) = e^(−2)·e^(−6) = e^(−8) ≈ 0.00034. By contrast, g(x,y) = 2 on 0 < x < y < 1 has marginals 2(1 − x) and 2y; their product 4y(1 − x) is not 2, so those two variables are dependent even though g looks simple.
chapters.trap: Deciding independence from the formula alone. 6e^(−2x−3y) splits into a function of x times a function of y, but many densities on a triangle also split — always check that the support is a rectangle.
chapters.leave: The relation between independence and zero covariance is settled in 4.4; independence of normal components in 4.7.

chapters.idea: Covariance is the average product of the two deviations from their means, so it is positive when X and Y rise together, negative when one rises as the other falls, and zero when there is no linear co-movement.
chapters.depth: Definition Cov(X,Y) = E[(X − μX)(Y − μY)] = E[XY] − μX μY, carrying units of X times units of Y. Properties: Cov(X,X) = Var(X), symmetry, bilinearity, Cov(aX + b, cY + d) = ac Cov(X,Y), and Var(X ± Y) = Var X + Var Y ± 2Cov(X,Y) for any X and Y. Joint moments E[X^i Y^j] and the joint mgf M(s,t) = E[e^(sX+tY)]. Correlation coefficient ρ = Cov(X,Y)/(σX σY), always between −1 and 1; its meaning as the slope of the best straight line, the regression line ŷ = μY + ρ(σY/σX)(x − μX). Independence gives ρ = 0, but ρ = 0 does not give independence outside the normal case. Some syllabi call ρ the coefficient of linear correlation.

figure.aria: Three straight lines through the origin with positive, zero and negative slopes, showing what the sign of the correlation coefficient looks like.

chapters.example: Take the two-dice table of 4.1, with X = number of 1s and Y = number of 2s. E[X] = E[Y] = 2(1/6) = 1/3. Only the pair (1,1) contributes to E[XY], so E[XY] = 1·1·(2/36) = 1/18. Then Cov(X,Y) = 1/18 − (1/3)(1/3) = −1/18 ≈ −0.056. Also Var(X) = Var(Y) = 2·(1/6)(5/6) = 5/18. Hence ρ = (−1/18)/(5/18) = −1/5 = −0.2: more 1s tends to mean fewer 2s.
chapters.trap: Concluding that ρ = 0 means independence. A second trap: writing Var(X + Y) = Var X + Var Y without the 2Cov(X,Y) term when the variables are not independent.
chapters.prereq: 4.1 to 4.3; expectation and variance from Unit 2; the regression line from Unit 1.
chapters.leave: Multiple and logistic regression in Unit 1; covariance matrices and their properties in 4.7; autocorrelation in Unit 7.

chapters.idea: With more and more independent observations, the sample mean gets closer and closer to the population mean, and the chance of any fixed-size gap goes to zero.
chapters.depth: Statement of the weak law for iid variables with finite mean μ and finite variance σ²: for every ε > 0, P(|X̄_n − μ| ≥ ε) → 0 as n → ∞. The proof by Chebyshev's inequality, using E[X̄_n] = μ and Var(X̄_n) = σ²/n, which gives the explicit bound σ²/(nε²). The strong law (X̄_n → μ almost surely) stated without proof. Sample proportion as the special case. Applications: why an opinion poll of a few thousand people can estimate a national proportion, why insurance works, Monte Carlo estimation of an integral. What the law does not say — it does not make past tosses even out.

figure.aria: A running average of coin tosses wandering above and below the true mean 0.4 and settling close to it as the number of tosses grows.

chapters.example: A coin lands heads with probability p = 0.4. After n = 2500 tosses, bound the chance that the observed proportion X̄ differs from 0.4 by 0.02 or more. Var(X̄) = p(1 − p)/n = 0.24/2500 = 0.000096. Chebyshev gives P(|X̄ − 0.4| ≥ 0.02) ≤ 0.000096/(0.02)² = 0.000096/0.0004 = 0.24. The true chance is much smaller; the bound is loose but needs no assumption about the shape of the distribution.
chapters.trap: Reading the law as a balancing rule, so that a tail is 'due' after ten heads. The proportion converges to p; the difference between the number of heads and the number of tails still grows like √n.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2: expectation, variance and Chebyshev's inequality.
chapters.leave: The exact shape of the error around μ is 4.6; unbiasedness and consistency of estimators in Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Add up many independent random variables with the same distribution and the standardized sum is approximately standard normal, whatever the parent distribution was.
chapters.depth: Statement for iid X₁, …, X_n with mean μ and finite variance σ²: (S_n − nμ)/(σ√n) → N(0,1) in distribution, where S_n = X₁ + … + X_n. Using it: P(S_n ≤ a) ≈ Φ((a − nμ)/(σ√n)), and the sample-mean form (X̄_n − μ)/(σ/√n) ≈ N(0,1). Continuity correction when S_n is a sum of whole numbers: use a ± 0.5. Normal approximation to the binomial as the special case, and how large n should be (the n ≥ 30 rule of thumb, and why skewness decides). Rates of convergence and exact error bounds are not covered.

figure.aria: The standard normal curve with the standardized binomial probabilities for ten trials sitting almost on top of it.

chapters.example: A fair coin is tossed 100 times and X is the number of heads. Estimate P(40 ≤ X ≤ 60) by the central limit theorem. Here μ = 100(0.5) = 50 and σ = √(100·0.5·0.5) = 5. With continuity correction the limits become 39.5 and 60.5, so z = ±(60.5 − 50)/5 = ±2.1 and the estimate is 2Φ(2.1) − 1 = 2(0.9821) − 1 = 0.9642. Without the correction, z = ±2 gives 0.9544.
chapters.trap: Standardizing with σ instead of σ√n, which makes the answer far too confident. Second trap: forgetting that the normal curve is continuous, so a sum of counts needs the ±0.5 correction before the table is read.
chapters.prereq: 4.5; the normal distribution and the table of Φ from Unit 3; binomial distribution from Unit 3.
chapters.leave: Exact sampling distributions (chi-square, t, F) in Unit 5; the large-sample tests built on this approximation in Unit 6.

chapters.idea: A random vector is multivariate normal when every linear combination of its parts is normal, and then the mean vector and the covariance matrix carry the whole distribution.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this chapter. Random vector X = (X₁, …, X_n)ᵀ, mean vector μ = E[X], covariance matrix Σ with Σ_ij = Cov(X_i, X_j), which is symmetric and positive semidefinite. Definition through the joint density f(x) = (2π)^(−n/2)|Σ|^(−1/2) exp(−½(x − μ)ᵀΣ⁻¹(x − μ)) when Σ is invertible, and through the characteristic function otherwise. The bivariate case written out with σ₁, σ₂ and ρ, whose contours are ellipses. Marginals and conditionals are again normal; in the bivariate case E[Y|X = x] = μY + ρ(σY/σX)(x − μX) and Var(Y|X = x) = σY²(1 − ρ²). Linear maps: if Y = AX + b then Y ~ N(Aμ + b, AΣAᵀ). Uncorrelated normal components are independent, unlike the general case. Decorrelation with Σ^(−1/2).

figure.aria: A normal vector stays normal under a linear map, and a further transformation removes the correlation and leaves independent normal components.

chapters.example: (X, Y) is bivariate normal with μX = 1, μY = 2, σX = 1, σY = 2 and ρ = 0.5. Find Σ, the conditional mean and variance of Y given X = 2, and P(Y > 3 | X = 2). Answer: Cov(X,Y) = ρσXσY = 0.5·1·2 = 1, so Σ = [[1, 1], [1, 4]] and |Σ| = 4 − 1 = 3. Conditional mean = 2 + 0.5(2)(2 − 1) = 3. Conditional variance = 4(1 − 0.25) = 3. The conditional law of Y is normal with mean 3 and variance 3, so P(Y > 3 | X = 2) = 0.5.
chapters.trap: Using σY² as the conditional variance instead of σY²(1 − ρ²). And applying the rule 'uncorrelated means independent' to vectors that are not multivariate normal — there it is false.
chapters.prereq: 4.1 to 4.4; the normal distribution from Unit 3.
chapters.leave: Estimating μ and Σ from data in Unit 5; Gaussian processes and noise in Unit 7; principal component analysis belongs to courses that cover multivariate statistics separately.
